title: The Leader You're Looking For Is Hiding in Plain Sight
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Drawing on a career that began as a state-government intern and continued through founding the Michigan Political Leadership Program and fifteen years teaching political leadership at George Washington University, Schafer argues that holding institutional authority is not the same thing as leading. She recounts repeatedly watching people with formal power become consumed by preserving it, while real change consistently came from people no one had given a title: a colleague who spoke up in a meeting, a junior staffer willing to go on the record, a neighbor who organized a needed change. Her argument culminates in a warning against outsourcing leadership to a small class of officials and public figures, and a call for readers to recognize the leadership they are already exercising in their own homes, workplaces, and communities rather than waiting for someone else to act.
points: Her formative realization: holding institutional authority did not necessarily mean someone was leading, since people with power could become consumed with preserving it rather than using it to fix what was visibly broken.

Leadership repeatedly appeared in people with no formal title — a colleague speaking up in a meeting, a junior staffer going on the record, a neighbor organizing a needed change — rather than in the people holding official positions.

Her core warning: 'America cannot afford to make leadership the responsibility of a relatively small group of people,' given more than 340 million citizens whose leadership capacity goes largely untapped.
She closes with three reflection questions designed to get readers to notice influence they're already exercising, rather than waiting for permission or a title before acting.
quotes: I also began to understand something I hadn’t anticipated: holding a position of authority did not necessarily mean someone was leading. People with enormous institutional power could become consumed with preserving that power, navigating the next election, protecting a department, defending an old decision, managing competing interests or simply keeping a system moving.

Again and again, leadership often appeared in places where no one had bestowed the title: a colleague speaking up in a meeting; a junior member going on the record when senior members would not; a neighbor organizing and advocating for a change everyone knew was needed; one person willing to have the conversation everyone else had been avoiding.

America cannot afford to make leadership the responsibility of a relatively small group of people. There are more than 340 million of us. Imagine the capacity we leave untouched when most of us assume leadership belongs primarily to someone else.

As John Lewis reminded us, “You must be bold, brave, and courageous and find a way… to get in the way.” Leadership is present whenever we recognize that what we do can affect what happens next, and decide to act accordingly.

My high school civics teacher probably had no idea what would follow from his suggestion that I spend my afternoons working for a local state legislator. He didn’t need to know. He saw something, cared enough to act and created an opening for me to discover what I could do.
